issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Mateo is a 70-year-old welder who has lived in the same small house for forty years, the one he shared with his wife until her passing two years ago. He is a man of immense physical strength, his hands calloused and powerful from a lifetime of shaping steel, but he speaks in a quiet, almost deferential tone. He has come to therapy after decades of silence, carrying a story from his youth as a student activist in his home country, a story that has governed every day of his life since.

Nearly fifty years ago, he was taken to a clandestine detention center. The narrative he provides is fragmented, punctuated by long pauses and the clenching of his fists. He speaks of a windowless room, the overwhelming sense of having no options, of being utterly trapped. It was this feeling of complete helplessness, more than the physical violence he endured, that broke something in him. He remembers the guards' casual cruelty and, most vividly, the sharp, flat crack of a gunshot from an adjoining cell-a sound that signaled an end he was sure would soon be his own. He was eventually released, but a part of him never left that room.

The memory did not fade with time; it remained immediate and raw. For Mateo, the event never settled into the past. When it returns, it is not a recollection but a re-experiencing; the air in his workshop grows thick and suffocating, and the smell of ozone from his welder feels like the metallic scent of blood and fear. A white-hot rage surges through him, so intense he has to put down his tools for fear of what his hands might do. He has never been able to tell the full story to anyone, not even his wife. When he tries, he says he loses the thread, the words dissolving as the visceral sensations take over, leaving him mute and shaking. Because the memory remains so immediate and sensory, he has become acutely sensitive to anything that echoes its core elements-sudden, sharp noises, or any situation where he feels his options are being taken away.

Over the years, these unprocessed memories calcified into a rigid set of beliefs about himself and the world. He became certain that his capture was his own fault, a direct result of his youthful arrogance and the way he acted. This self-blame is twinned with a profound and unrelenting guilt; he will never forgive himself for not doing more, for not fighting back harder to stop what was happening. These convictions have bled into his perception of the world today, leaving him with the core belief that you can never know who will harm you, that danger is arbitrary and can emerge from anywhere, from anyone.

This constellation of fear and memory is easily ignited. A car backfiring on the street outside his workshop is not just a startling noise; for Mateo, it is the gunshot from the next cell. The sound instantly plunges him back into the memory, the feeling of the cold floor beneath him, the rage coiling in his gut. The trigger also serves as immediate confirmation of his negative appraisals: the world is indeed a dangerous place, and threat is ever-present. He feels a deep sense of shame in these moments, a fresh wave of self-blame for being so weak.

His life has become organized around managing these intrusions. Because he believes that anyone can be a source of harm, any situation that feels confrontational or entrapping activates a desperate need to de-escalate. When a client recently cornered him in the shop to aggressively dispute a bill-a clear trigger of feeling trapped with no options-Mateo found himself becoming overly compliant, agreeing to an unfair discount just to make the man leave. In the aftermath of such encounters, and whenever the memories surface on their own, he engages in a punishing internal battle, trying to suppress the thoughts and detach himself from the feelings, a strategy that leaves him feeling hollowed out and exhausted.

The cycle is now deeply entrenched and self-perpetuating. His belief that the world is a hostile place keeps him in a state of constant vigilance, which in turn makes him hyper-sensitive to the very triggers he dreads. The sheer horror of the memories themselves-the rage, the terror-has also made him phobic of his own mind. He actively avoids anything that might lead him back to that room, from news reports about political unrest to movies with any hint of violence. His world has shrunk to his workshop and his home, a perimeter he patrols with anxious care.

It was his grandson who finally broke through the wall of his avoidance. The boy, curious about the faded scars on his grandfather's arms, asked him where they came from. Mateo was met with the familiar paralysis: the inability to explain, the sudden, inexplicable rage, and the profound shame that followed. The look of fear in his grandson's eyes was the catalyst. He has come to therapy now, terrified of what unearthing the past will do to him, but more terrified of dying with this poison still inside him.
